name: The Trie
statement: Store strings in a tree where the path from the root spells the key, so shared prefixes are shared.
statementAccent: the path from the root spells the key
meaning: A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a tree data structure used to store and retrieve a set of strings, in which the position of a node in the tree defines the key associated with it. Unlike a binary search tree, a trie does not store keys directly in its nodes; instead, a node's position, that is, the path from the root down to it, spells out the key. Each edge represents a character, or symbol, and so all the descendants of a node share the common prefix spelled by the path from the root to that node, which is why it is called a prefix tree; the root represents the empty string, and certain nodes are marked to indicate the end of a valid key. The name trie comes from the middle of the word retrieval, coined by Edward Fredkin around 1960; it is commonly pronounced like try to distinguish it in speech from tree, though Fredkin himself pronounced it like tree. A key performance feature is that looking up or inserting a key of length m takes time proportional to m, independent of the number of keys stored in the trie, which can be faster than a binary search tree for string keys, although tries can consume a lot of memory. Tries are used for autocomplete and predictive text, spell checking, IP routing by longest-prefix matching, and storing and searching strings by prefix. Compressed variants include the radix tree and the Patricia trie.
mechanism: A trie encodes a set of strings in the shape of a tree, so that the identity of a key is given not by data stored in a node but by the sequence of edges leading to it from the root. Each edge is labelled with a single character from the alphabet, and each node corresponds to the string formed by concatenating the edge labels along the path from the root; the root itself corresponds to the empty string. Because a node's string is the common prefix of all strings in its subtree, every descendant shares that prefix, and strings that share a beginning share the whole initial path through the tree, branching apart only where they first differ. Some nodes carry a marker indicating that the string spelled to that point is a full, stored key, as opposed to merely a prefix of longer keys. To look up a string, one starts at the root and follows, character by character, the edge matching each successive character of the string; if at any point the needed edge is missing, the string is absent, and if the final node is marked as a key, the string is present. Insertion follows the same descent, creating any missing edges and nodes along the way and marking the final node. The crucial efficiency property is that these operations touch one node per character, so the time for a key of length m is proportional to m, regardless of how many keys the trie holds, in contrast to comparison-based structures whose cost grows with the number of keys. The price is memory: each node may need a slot or pointer for every possible next character, so sparse tries can waste space, which motivates compressed forms. Radix trees, or Patricia tries, collapse chains of single-child nodes into single edges labelled with multi-character strings, greatly reducing the node count.

examples.text: Each edge is a character, and the path from the root to a node spells the string that node represents.
All descendants of a node share the prefix spelled to that node, so common beginnings share a path.
Finding a key of length m takes time proportional to m, independent of how many keys the trie holds.

whyItMatters: The trie is a foundational data structure for working with strings, the natural way to store and search a set of words or keys organized by their prefixes, and it powers many features people use constantly. Because a trie shares the common prefixes of its keys along shared paths, it makes prefix-based operations extremely natural and fast: finding every stored word that begins with a given prefix is simply a matter of walking to the node for that prefix and reading off its subtree. This is exactly what autocomplete and predictive text need, and tries, or their compressed relatives, underlie the suggestions that appear as one types in search boxes, phones, and editors, as well as spell checkers and dictionaries. A different but equally important use is in network routers, where longest-prefix matching over IP addresses, essential to routing packets, is performed with trie structures. The trie's defining performance property, that lookup and insertion cost scale with the length of the key rather than the number of keys, makes it especially attractive when many strings share structure, and its compressed forms, the radix tree and Patricia trie, tame its memory appetite. Named by Edward Fredkin from the middle of the word retrieval around 1960, the trie remains a core tool for string processing. As the tree in which the path from the root spells the key and prefixes are shared, the trie is a cornerstone of string data structures.

limits: The trie is excellent for prefix-structured strings but has limits that reward care. Its most cited drawback is memory: because each node may need capacity for every possible next character, a naive trie over a large alphabet or with few shared prefixes can consume far more space than the strings themselves, which is why compressed variants, the radix tree and Patricia trie, are often used in practice; the memory cost is a general trade-off rather than a fixed rule, since for many short strings a trie can also be compact. The length-proportional lookup time, order m for a key of length m, is an advantage for strings but means the trie is tied to sequential-symbol keys and does not generalize to arbitrary comparable keys the way a binary search tree does. Tries also do not by themselves keep keys in a comparison order beyond the lexicographic order implied by their paths. A naming nuance rewards care: Edward Fredkin coined trie from retrieval around 1960 and pronounced it like tree, while the common pronunciation like try arose to distinguish it in speech, so attributing the try pronunciation to Fredkin is inaccurate; and the concept was first described by René de la Briandais in 1959. So the trie robustly stores and searches strings by prefix, understood as a structure whose speed suits string keys and whose memory cost motivates its compressed variants.
misreadings: The trie does not store keys in its nodes; the path from the root spells the key. It is not automatically memory-cheap, since sparse tries can waste much space, motivating compressed forms. And it is specialized for string keys, not a general comparison structure, so treating a trie as storing keys in nodes, as always compact, or as a drop-in for any ordered map, misreads it.
origin: The prefix-tree data structure, named by Edward Fredkin from retrieval around 1960, in which the path from the root spells each string key and common prefixes are shared.
